newsitem.title: GERMANY: Gene-soya row unlikely to change EU trade flows.
newsitem.headline: Gene-soya row unlikely to change EU trade flows.

text.p: A wave of protests against genetically altered U.S. soybeans in Europe will underpin domestic rapeseed oil prices and keep bureaucrats busy with labelling requests, industry sources said on Wednesday.
But the row looks unlikely to disturb flows of soybeans, oil and meal in and out of the EU in the 1996/97 season.
"Opportunists in the food and feeds industries have found short-term ways around the problem," an oilseeds broker said.
"The bolder ones feel safe to stay out of the emotional debate and get on with business -- they may well have a point."
EU oilseeds processors operating a powerful capacity of about 30 million tonnes a year need imported soybeans to produce enough oils and meals for the home market and overseas.

"U.S. shipments to Europe will continue," said Arnd von Wissel, managing director of oil mill Oelmuehle Hamburg, where campaigners protested at the arrival of new crop U.S. beans and tried to block the despatch of products.
"The U.S. will be the only shop in town until next spring and if the beans aren't processed here, they will go to Belgium or the Netherlands," von Wissel said.
Led by environmentalist group Greenpeace, the opponents say the new beans are a hazardous experiment with nature, although they have been given a clean bill of health in the U.S. and EU.
Developer U.S. chemicals firm Monsanto has made them resistant to its weedkiller roundup.
German trader Toepfer sees the EU importing 13.6 million tonnes of soybeans in 96/97 and crushing 13.2 million, little less than in 95/96 at 14.0 and 13.6 million respectively.
With world demand for oilseeds and products accelerating, the EU needs to buy from the 65.4 million tonne U.S. soy crop.
Animal feeds brokers said demand for soymeal had not fallen as the protein-rich feed became associated with the gene row.
"Forward dates are being ordered and genetically natural old crop soymeal finds no takers at a higher price," one said.
But one result of the concern over gene-soya will be a sustained rape oil premium over soy oil, traders agreed.
The premium, currently at 5.0-5.50 guilders, developed amid tight rapeseed supply and as leading food firms bought rape oil instead of soy oil to guard against possible consumer anger.

"I think the premium will be maintained, but all it means is that crushers will ship relatively more soy oil to overseas customers, where European prices are competitive," said Arnold F Mergell of the German crushers association VDO.
And a spokesman at the German subsidiary of Anglo-Dutch Unilever said the company would prefer rape oil for its margarine as long as it was on offer and the row continued.
He said the firm, which buys some 120,000 tonnes of oil a year, believed soya was safe and was merely bowing to pressure.
Another long-term effect of the consumer crisis will be calls on legislators at national and EU level to find acceptable ways of labelling bio-engineered products.

"The labelling debate has to become more pro-active and progressive, to offer consumers choices and to inform them about the positive aspects of biotechnology," said Hans-Juergen Bertram, managing director of German oilseeds lobby UFOP.

Another Greenpeace demand -- the segregationg of transgenic and conventional soybeans at origin -- was unlikely to succeed because of extra costs and as suppliers were not established enough to gain trust from EU crushers, traders said.
They also said the European Commission was likely to delay decisions on whether to allow modified U.S. maize into the EU and when to allow domestic production of gene-altered rapeseed.
Meanwhile, sales of modified soybean seeds have begun in Argentina and Brazil also has plans to begin production soon.
